extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, media policymakers, media-support organisations and the interested public
extracted.subtask_description: High-level principles and practical standards for professional journalism in the digital age, emphasising core values, governance, platform responsibility and public trust. Covers what journalists, newsrooms and platforms should do to preserve accuracy, independence and civic purpose amid technological and commercial pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core values: accuracy, independence and responsible reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The core values of accuracy, independence and responsible reporting remain as relevant as ever and should continue to guide journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These values have evolved over the past 150 years and are foundational to building public trust. Newsrooms should prioritise fact-checking, avoid undue influence and maintain editorial independence even under commercial and political pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-based communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism must be fact-based: reporting should be grounded in verified facts rather than speculation or unverified content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fact-based reporting helps expose fake news and provides a basis for policy to build a safe and reliable public information space. Journalists should verify information, debunk falsehoods where possible, and provide context that helps audiences understand the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanity and respect for others
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting should demonstrate humanity and show respect for people affected by news coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes careful language, sensitivity to victims and affected communities, and avoiding dehumanising or inflammatory descriptions. Ethical restraint should be practised by journalists and everyone participating in the public information sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and owning up to errors
rubrics_metrics.description: News organisations should be transparent and willing to acknowledge and correct mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owning up to errors strengthens credibility and trust. Corrections and transparent editorial processes should be visible to audiences as part of ethical accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid political bias, undue corporate influence, stereotypes and conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism should guard against political bias, corporate interference, stereotyping and conflicts of interest that distort reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms must identify and manage conflicts, maintain editorial independence from political and commercial pressures, and actively work to prevent stereotyping in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote information literacy through partnership with audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Media should work with audiences and policymakers to promote information literacy so the public can better assess and use information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EJN argues for new partnerships to persuade publics and policymakers of the value of ethical journalism and to design programmes that raise audience ability to distinguish reliable information from misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical restraint should be voluntary, not legally imposed
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical values and restraint in communications should be pursued voluntarily rather than enforced by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While governments may propose fines or laws to force platforms to remove malicious content, such legal measures risk limiting legitimate dissent and free speech; voluntary commitments by platforms and publics are preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism's civic purpose and role in building public trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism has a civic purpose: it is essential for democracy and for building and maintaining public trust in the information environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because journalism is fact-based and serves civic ends, it can inform policy-making and help create a safer public information space. News organisations should emphasise public-interest reporting even when business models are under strain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human oversight over algorithmic distribution and ethical decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical decisions about information should be handled by trained, informed human journalists and editors rather than solely by algorithms or automated systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithms prioritise engagement (clicks, virality) not ethics; digital robots can't be encoded with full ethical and moral values. Human editorial oversight is needed to judge context, nuance and harms—content moderation at scale (e.g., Facebook’s thousands of reviewers) remains insufficient without professional journalistic input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platforms' responsibility to recognise journalism as a public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology companies should accept a publisher-like role in the digital age and support professional journalism as a public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms can deploy resources (e.g., employ or contract ethical journalists) to help moderate and promote reliable information instead of treating journalism the same as other content in their marketing and algorithms. The article cites platform wealth and the feasibility of such investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist misuse of technology to exploit privacy and manipulate politics
rubrics_metrics.description: The exploitation of people’s privacy and targeted marketing of false information (e.g., political adverts micro-targeting) is unethical and poses democratic risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include mass variations of political adverts on Facebook and use of hacked or artificially created email dumps in elections; journalists and policymakers should highlight and guard against techniques that manipulate voters or spread malicious misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose and counter fake news while respecting legal constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should investigate, verify and expose fake news, but must operate within the bounds of law (e.g., election-period publication restrictions) and rely on professional processes to assess material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article references situations (France election email leaks) where legal restrictions limited journalists’ ability to examine material; when possible, newsrooms should provide verification and context to prevent the spread of false material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen ethics and governance through training and practical actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Media organisations and networks should invest in training, guidelines and practical tools to strengthen journalistic ethics and governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EJN’s activities—developing tests to expose hate speech, guidelines on reporting conflict, and producing reports on migration coverage—are cited as examples of concrete steps to bolster standards and self-regulation within media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical standards apply to all participants in the public information sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only professional journalists but also citizen journalists, social media users and platform actors should be guided by ethical principles like fact-based communication, respect and transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EJN argues these cardinal principles should guide everyone, though via voluntary adoption rather than legal compulsion; education and norms-setting are implied methods to extend standards beyond professional newsrooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to commercial incentives that favour sensationalism and click-driven content
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial business models that reward virality and clicks incentivise sensational, provocative or unethical content over truth and public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms’ algorithms and advertising-driven incentives make sensationalism profitable; news organisations and platforms should recognise and mitigate these incentives to preserve ethical reporting.
